*This page follows @bertsimas2004, "The Price of Robustness". Background on uncertainty
sets and the earlier box and ellipsoid models is on
[Uncertainty Sets and Robust Counterparts](introduction.qmd); notes on the paper itself are
on [Bertsimas & Sim (2004)](papers/bertsimas-2004.qmd).*

## The idea

The box model of @soyster1973 protects a constraint against *every* uncertain coefficient
taking its worst value at the same time. When the errors are independent this almost never
happens: some coefficients come out high, some low, and the errors partly cancel. Protecting
against the full worst case gives up a lot of objective for very little real benefit.

@bertsimas2004 proposed a middle ground. For each constraint $i$ the modeller picks a
number $\Gamma_i$, the *budget of uncertainty*, and the solution is protected against any
$\Gamma_i$ of the row's coefficients going to their worst values at once. Nature can spoil
some coefficients, but not all of them.

- $\Gamma_i = 0$ gives the nominal problem: no protection.
- $\Gamma_i$ equal to the number of uncertain coefficients gives Soyster's box model: full
  protection.
- Values in between trade objective for protection, one constraint at a time. $\Gamma_i$
  does not have to be an integer.

**Tiny example.** Row 1 of the toy LP from the [previous page](introduction.qmd) is
$(2 \pm 0.6)\,x_1 + (1 \pm 0.5)\,x_2 \le 10$ with $x \ge 0$. With $\Gamma_1 = 1$, only one of
the two coefficients can go wrong, and nature picks whichever hurts more at the current $x$:
the extra load is $\max(0.6\,x_1,\; 0.5\,x_2)$. So the robust row is

$$
2x_1 + x_2 + \max(0.6\,x_1,\ 0.5\,x_2) \le 10
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
2.6\,x_1 + x_2 \le 10 \;\text{ and }\; 2x_1 + 1.5\,x_2 \le 10 ,
$$

which is still linear. With $\Gamma_1 = 2$ both coefficients go wrong and the row becomes
Soyster's $2.6\,x_1 + 1.5\,x_2 \le 10$.

## The model

Start from a nominal LP

$$
\max\; c^\top x \quad\text{s.t.}\quad Ax \le b,\quad l \le x \le u .
$$

In row $i$, let $J_i$ be the set of coefficients that are uncertain. Each
$\tilde a_{ij}$, $j \in J_i$, lies in $[\bar a_{ij} - \hat a_{ij},\ \bar a_{ij} + \hat a_{ij}]$
around its nominal value $\bar a_{ij}$. Pick $\Gamma_i \in [0, \lvert J_i\rvert]$. The robust
model of @bertsimas2004 is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\max\;& c^\top x\\
\text{s.t. }& \sum_j \bar a_{ij}\, x_j + \beta_i(x, \Gamma_i) \le b_i \qquad i = 1,\dots,m,\\
& l \le x \le u,
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-bs-model}

with the *protection function*

$$
\beta_i(x, \Gamma_i) \;=\;
\max_{\substack{S_i \subseteq J_i,\ \lvert S_i\rvert = \lfloor\Gamma_i\rfloor\\ t_i \in J_i \setminus S_i}}
\Big\{ \sum_{j \in S_i} \hat a_{ij}\,\lvert x_j\rvert \;+\; (\Gamma_i - \lfloor\Gamma_i\rfloor)\,\hat a_{i t_i}\lvert x_{t_i}\rvert \Big\}.
$$ {#eq-protection}

In words: sort the possible damages $\hat a_{ij}\lvert x_j\rvert$ from largest to smallest;
$\beta_i$ is the sum of the $\lfloor\Gamma_i\rfloor$ largest, plus the fraction
$\Gamma_i - \lfloor\Gamma_i\rfloor$ of the next one. It is the worst extra load on row $i$
when $\lfloor\Gamma_i\rfloor$ coefficients go fully wrong and one more goes partly wrong.

As written, @eq-bs-model is not an LP: $\beta_i$ is a maximum over subsets. The next section
removes the maximum.

## From a max inside a constraint to an LP

**Step 1: the subset choice is an LP** [@bertsimas2004, Proposition 1]. For a fixed $x$,

$$
\beta_i(x, \Gamma_i) \;=\; \max\Big\{ \sum_{j \in J_i} \hat a_{ij}\lvert x_j\rvert\, z_{ij} \;:\;
\sum_{j \in J_i} z_{ij} \le \Gamma_i,\ \ 0 \le z_{ij} \le 1 \Big\}.
$$ {#eq-beta-lp}

The feasible set is a box cut by one budget constraint. Filling the budget greedily, with
$z_{ij} = 1$ on the largest damages and a fractional $z$ on the next one, is optimal, and
that is exactly @eq-protection. Read $z_{ij}$ as "how much coefficient $j$ deviates", so
@eq-beta-lp is the worst case over the uncertainty set
$U_i(\Gamma_i) = \{\bar a_i + \hat a_i \circ \eta : \lVert\eta\rVert_\infty \le 1,\ \lVert\eta\rVert_1 \le \Gamma_i\}$
drawn in @fig-budget-sets.

**Step 2: dualize.** @eq-beta-lp is a feasible, bounded LP, so by LP duality its value
equals the value of its dual,

$$
\beta_i(x, \Gamma_i) \;=\; \min\Big\{ \Gamma_i\, z_i + \sum_{j \in J_i} p_{ij} \;:\;
z_i + p_{ij} \ge \hat a_{ij}\lvert x_j\rvert \ \ \forall j \in J_i,\ \ z_i \ge 0,\ p_{ij} \ge 0 \Big\}.
$$ {#eq-beta-dual}

**Step 3: drop the min.** A constraint "something $+$ a minimum $\le b_i$" holds exactly when
*some* feasible dual point satisfies it, so the minimization can be merged into the outer
problem. Writing $\lvert x_j\rvert \le y_j$ with $-y_j \le x_j \le y_j$ gives the robust
counterpart.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Theorem 1** [@bertsimas2004]. Model @eq-bs-model is equivalent to the linear program

$$
\begin{aligned}
\max\;& c^\top x\\
\text{s.t. }& \sum_j \bar a_{ij} x_j + \Gamma_i z_i + \sum_{j \in J_i} p_{ij} \le b_i && \forall i\\
& z_i + p_{ij} \ge \hat a_{ij}\, y_j && \forall i,\ j \in J_i\\
& -y_j \le x_j \le y_j && \forall j\\
& l \le x \le u,\quad p_{ij} \ge 0,\ y_j \ge 0,\ z_i \ge 0 .
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-bs-lp}
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Proof

*If $(x, y, z, p)$ is feasible for @eq-bs-lp, then $x$ is feasible for @eq-bs-model.* Since
$y_j \ge \lvert x_j\rvert$, the pair $(z_i, p_{i\cdot})$ is feasible for the dual
@eq-beta-dual at $x$. By weak duality, $\Gamma_i z_i + \sum_j p_{ij} \ge \beta_i(x, \Gamma_i)$,
so $\sum_j \bar a_{ij} x_j + \beta_i(x, \Gamma_i) \le b_i$.

*If $x$ is feasible for @eq-bs-model, it extends to a feasible point of @eq-bs-lp.* Put
$y_j = \lvert x_j\rvert$ and let $(z_i, p_{i\cdot})$ be an optimal solution of
the dual @eq-beta-dual. By strong duality its value is exactly $\beta_i(x, \Gamma_i)$, so the first
constraint of @eq-bs-lp holds.

The two problems have the same feasible $x$ and the same objective, so they are equivalent. $\square$
:::

**What the new variables mean.** For a fixed $x$, the best dual choice is a threshold:
$z_i$ is the $(\lfloor\Gamma_i\rfloor + 1)$-th largest damage and
$p_{ij} = (\hat a_{ij}\lvert x_j\rvert - z_i)^+$ is how far damage $j$ sticks out above it.
So $\beta_i = \min_{z \ge 0}\, \{\Gamma_i z + \sum_j (\hat a_{ij}\lvert x_j\rvert - z)^+\}$:
pay $z$ for each unit of budget, plus whatever exceeds the threshold.

**Why this matters.**

- The robust problem is an LP of the same kind as the nominal one. It adds one $z_i$ per
  row, one $p_{ij}$ per uncertain coefficient, and one $y_j$ per variable (none are needed
  when $x \ge 0$). Each new constraint touches only three variables, so the sparsity of $A$
  is kept.
- Nothing in the derivation used continuity of $x$. If some $x_j$ must be integer,
  @eq-bs-lp is a MIP with the same integer variables, and any MIP solver handles it. This
  is the main practical advantage over the ellipsoidal model, which turns a MIP into a
  mixed-integer conic program.

## How likely is a violation?

The model protects row $i$ *for certain* as long as at most $\lfloor\Gamma_i\rfloor$
coefficients deviate (and one more partly). What if more of them deviate? Suppose the
deviations are random:

$$
\tilde a_{ij} = \bar a_{ij} + \eta_{ij}\,\hat a_{ij}, \qquad
\eta_{ij} \text{ independent, symmetric around } 0, \text{ with values in } [-1, 1].
$$

Let $x^*$ be optimal for @eq-bs-lp and $n = \lvert J_i\rvert$. @bertsimas2004 prove two
bounds on the probability that row $i$ is violated at $x^*$.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Theorem 2** [@bertsimas2004]. $\displaystyle \Pr\Big(\sum_j \tilde a_{ij} x_j^* > b_i\Big) \le \exp\!\Big(-\frac{\Gamma_i^2}{2n}\Big).$

**Theorem 3** [@bertsimas2004]. $\displaystyle \Pr\Big(\sum_j \tilde a_{ij} x_j^* > b_i\Big) \le B(n, \Gamma_i)$, where

$$
B(n, \Gamma) = \frac{1}{2^n}\Big[(1 - \mu)\sum_{l = \lfloor\nu\rfloor}^{n} \binom{n}{l} + \mu \sum_{l = \lfloor\nu\rfloor + 1}^{n} \binom{n}{l}\Big],
\qquad \nu = \frac{\Gamma + n}{2},\quad \mu = \nu - \lfloor\nu\rfloor .
$$

The bound is tight: it is attained when the $\eta_{ij}$ are $\pm 1$ with probability $\tfrac12$
each (for integer $\Gamma_i \geq 1$ with $n + \Gamma_i$ even). For large $n$,
$B(n, \Gamma) \approx 1 - \Phi\big((\Gamma - 1)/\sqrt n\big)$, where $\Phi$ is the standard
normal distribution function.
:::

Two things stand out. First, **the bounds do not depend on $x^*$**: they depend only on
$\Gamma_i$ and on how many coefficients are uncertain. The modeller can choose $\Gamma_i$
from a target violation probability before solving anything. Second, **$\Gamma_i$ only has to
grow like $\sqrt n$**. A violation probability of $\varepsilon$ needs roughly
$\Gamma_i \approx 1 + \Phi^{-1}(1 - \varepsilon)\sqrt n$, a vanishing share of the $n$
coefficients when $n$ is large.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-gamma-needed
#| tbl-cap: "Smallest budget $\\Gamma$ with $B(n, \\Gamma)$ at most 1% or 0.1%, computed from Theorem 3. The share $\\Gamma/n$ falls like $1/\\sqrt n$."
rows = []
for n in (10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000):
    g1, g2 = gamma_for(n, 0.01), gamma_for(n, 0.001)
    rows.append(f"| {n} | {g1:.1f} | {100 * g1 / n:.0f}% | {g2:.1f} | {100 * g2 / n:.0f}% |")
Markdown("| $n$ uncertain coefficients | $\\Gamma$ for 1% | $\\Gamma / n$ | $\\Gamma$ for 0.1% | $\\Gamma / n$ |\n"
         "|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|\n" + "\n".join(rows))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Proof sketch of Theorem 2

Write $d_j = \hat a_{ij}\lvert x^*_j\rvert$ for the possible damages and drop the index $i$.
Because each $\eta_j$ is symmetric, flipping its sign when $x^*_j < 0$ does not change any
probability, so row $i$ is violated with probability
$\Pr\big(\sum_j \eta_j d_j > \beta(x^*, \Gamma)\big)$, using
$\sum_j \bar a_j x^*_j + \beta \le b$.

*Reduce to a sum with unit weights* [@bertsimas2004, Proposition 2]. Let $S^*$ and $t^*$ be the
maximizers in @eq-protection, so $\beta = \sum_{j \in S^*} d_j + (\Gamma - \lfloor\Gamma\rfloor)d_{t^*}$,
and let $d_{r}$ be the smallest damage among $S^* \cup \{t^*\}$ (assume $d_r > 0$). Every
damage outside $S^*$ is at most $d_r$. Then

$$
\sum_j \eta_j d_j - \beta
= \sum_{j \in S^*} (\eta_j - 1) d_j + \sum_{j \notin S^*} \eta_j d_j - (\Gamma - \lfloor\Gamma\rfloor) d_{t^*}
\le d_r\Big[\sum_{j \in S^*} (\eta_j - 1) + \sum_{j \notin S^*} \mu_j \eta_j - (\Gamma - \lfloor\Gamma\rfloor)\Big],
$$

with weights $\mu_j = d_j / d_r \le 1$ (using $\eta_j - 1 \le 0$ and $d_j \ge d_r$ on $S^*$). So a
violation forces $\sum_j \mu_j \eta_j > \Gamma$, with $\mu_j = 1$ on $S^*$ and
$\mu_j \le 1$ elsewhere.

*Bound that event.* For any $\theta > 0$, by Markov's inequality and independence,

$$
\Pr\Big(\sum_j \mu_j \eta_j \ge \Gamma\Big)
\le e^{-\theta\Gamma}\prod_j \mathbb{E}\big[e^{\theta\mu_j\eta_j}\big]
\le e^{-\theta\Gamma}\prod_j \cosh(\theta)
\le e^{-\theta\Gamma + n\theta^2/2}.
$$

The middle step uses symmetry ($\mathbb{E}[e^{s\eta}] = \mathbb{E}[\cosh(s\eta)] \le \cosh s$
for $\lvert\eta\rvert \le 1$, $\lvert s\rvert \le \theta$) and the last uses
$\cosh\theta \le e^{\theta^2/2}$. Choosing $\theta = \Gamma/n$ gives $e^{-\Gamma^2/(2n)}$.
Theorem 3 sharpens the second step by comparing with the worst case, symmetric $\pm 1$
variables, and counting binomial outcomes.
:::

## The price of robustness: a knapsack experiment

How much objective does protection cost in a problem with many uncertain coefficients? The
following experiment is in the spirit of Section 6.1 of @bertsimas2004, on our own random
instance. There are 200 items with nominal weights drawn from $\{20, \dots, 29\}$ and values
from $\{16, \dots, 77\}$, a capacity of 4000, and every weight uncertain by $\pm 10\%$:

$$
\max \sum_j c_j x_j \quad\text{s.t.}\quad \sum_j \tilde w_j x_j \le 4000, \quad x \in \{0, 1\}^{200}.
$$

For each $\Gamma$ we solve the robust counterpart @eq-bs-lp (a MIP; $y = x$ since $x \ge 0$)
and then draw 20,000 random weight vectors to see how often the chosen load really exceeds
the capacity.

```{python}
#| label: knapsack-runs
#| output: false
c, w, what, cap = knapsack_instance()
N = len(c)
GK = list(range(0, 61, 2)) + list(range(70, 201, 10))
KN = []
for g in GK:
    xg, vg = robust_knapsack(c, w, what, cap, g)
    KN.append(dict(g=g, v=vg, items=int(xg.sum()),
                   sim_pm=violation_rate(xg, w, what, cap, kind="pm1"),
                   sim_un=violation_rate(xg, w, what, cap, kind="uniform"),
                   B=bound_B(N, g), E=bound_exp(N, g)))
V0 = KN[0]["v"]
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-knapsack
#| fig-cap: "The price of robustness on a 200-item knapsack. Left: loss of objective relative to the nominal solution. Right: probability that the robust solution overloads the knapsack: the bounds of Theorems 2 and 3 (lines) and simulated rates for $\\pm 1$ and uniform deviations (markers; rates below 1 in 20,000 are not shown). Notice that the bound reaches 1% while the objective has dropped by only about 1%; full protection costs several times more."
G = np.array([r["g"] for r in KN])
loss = np.array([100 * (V0 - r["v"]) / V0 for r in KN])
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4))
ax = axes[0]
ax.plot(G, loss, "-o", color=COLORS["p1"], ms=3.5)
ax.axhline(loss[-1], color=COLORS["weak"], ls=":", lw=1.2)
ax.text(200, loss[-1] + 0.15, f"Soyster (full protection): {loss[-1]:.1f}%", ha="right",
        color=COLORS["weak"], fontsize=9.5)
ax.set_xlabel(r"budget $\Gamma$"); ax.set_ylabel("objective loss vs. nominal (%)")
ax.set_ylim(0, loss[-1] * 1.25); ax.grid(True, color=COLORS["grid"], lw=0.5, alpha=0.5)

ax = axes[1]
gg = np.linspace(0, 120, 241)
ax.semilogy(gg, [bound_exp(N, t) for t in gg], color=COLORS["grid"], lw=1.6, ls="--",
            label="Theorem 2: $e^{-\\Gamma^2/2n}$")
ax.semilogy(gg, [bound_B(N, t) for t in gg], color=COLORS["text"], lw=1.6,
            label=r"Theorem 3: $B(n, \Gamma)$")
pm = np.array([r["sim_pm"] for r in KN]); un = np.array([r["sim_un"] for r in KN])
ax.semilogy(G[pm > 0], pm[pm > 0], "o", color=COLORS["p2"], ms=4.5, label=r"simulated, $\pm 1$")
ax.semilogy(G[un > 0], un[un > 0], "s", color=COLORS["hull"], ms=4, label="simulated, uniform")
ax.set_xlim(0, 120); ax.set_ylim(1e-5, 1)
ax.set_xlabel(r"budget $\Gamma$"); ax.set_ylabel("probability of overload")
ax.grid(True, color=COLORS["grid"], lw=0.5, alpha=0.5, which="major")
ax.legend(fontsize=8.5, loc="upper right", frameon=True, framealpha=0.9)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-knapsack
#| tbl-cap: "Selected budgets from the knapsack experiment. The bound is $B(200, \\Gamma)$ from Theorem 3; the simulated rates use 20,000 draws."
pick = [0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 100, 200]
rows = []
for r in KN:
    if r["g"] in pick:
        rows.append(f"| {r['g']} | {r['v']:.0f} | {100 * (V0 - r['v']) / V0:.2f}% | {r['items']} | "
                    f"{r['B']:.2g} | {r['sim_pm']:.2g} | {r['sim_un']:.2g} |")
Markdown("| $\\Gamma$ | value | loss | items | bound $B$ | simulated $\\pm1$ | simulated uniform |\n"
         "|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|\n" + "\n".join(rows))
```

```{python}
#| label: knapsack-summary
#| output: asis
g1 = next(r for r in KN if r["B"] <= 0.01)
print(f"The pattern matches what @bertsimas2004 report for their instance. Here the nominal "
      f"solution overloads the knapsack about half the time. Full protection removes that risk "
      f"but loses {100 * (V0 - KN[-1]['v']) / V0:.1f}% of the value. The smallest budget on our "
      f"grid with a 1% guarantee, $\\Gamma = {g1['g']}$, loses only "
      f"{100 * (V0 - g1['v']) / V0:.2f}%. (In the paper, full protection cost 5.5% and a "
      f"guarantee of about 0.57% cost 1.54%.) The simulated rates sit below the bound, and "
      f"the $\\pm 1$ deviations, the worst case for Theorem 3, come closest to it.")
```

## Beyond the basic model

- **Discrete problems.** Because @eq-bs-lp keeps the problem class, the budget model is
  routinely used inside MIPs. For 0–1 problems whose *costs* are uncertain, @bertsimas2003
  showed that the robust problem can be solved by solving $n + 1$ nominal problems, so a
  polynomially solvable problem (shortest path, minimum spanning tree, ...) stays
  polynomially solvable.
- **Correlated data** [@bertsimas2004, Section 5]. If the coefficients of a row are driven
  by a few common factors, $\tilde a_{ij} = \bar a_{ij} + \sum_{k \in K_i} \eta_{ik} g_{kj}$,
  the budget is put on the factors $\eta_{ik}$ instead. The counterpart is again an LP, and
  the bound becomes $B(\lvert K_i\rvert, \Gamma_i)$.
- **Which budget to raise?** Under nondegeneracy, the derivative of the optimal value with
  respect to $\Gamma_i$ is $-z_i^* q_i^*$, where $z_i^*$ is the threshold variable of row $i$
  in @eq-bs-lp and $q_i^*$ is the dual price of that row [@bertsimas2004, Theorem 4]. Rows
  with a small product are cheap to protect.

## In practice

- **Pick $\Gamma_i$ from a target probability.** Choose the largest violation probability
  you can accept for row $i$, and read $\Gamma_i$ off
  $B(\lvert J_i\rvert, \Gamma_i)$, as in @tbl-gamma-needed. Joint guarantees for several rows follow from a union bound.
- **Many uncertain coefficients per row is where it pays.** The saving over Soyster comes
  from errors cancelling, which needs many of them. With only a handful of uncertain
  coefficients in a row, a meaningful guarantee needs $\Gamma_i$ close to
  $\lvert J_i\rvert$, and the result is close to the box model. @bertsimas2004 saw this on
  a NETLIB problem whose rows had at most 29 uncertain entries.
- **Check the assumptions.** The guarantees assume independent, symmetric, bounded
  deviations. The deterministic guarantee (any $\lfloor\Gamma_i\rfloor$ coefficients) holds
  without them.
- **Static decisions.** All of $x$ is chosen before the data are seen. Problems with
  recourse are closer to [stochastic programming](../stochastic-programming/index.qmd).

- Paper notes: [Bertsimas & Sim (2004), The Price of Robustness](papers/bertsimas-2004.qmd).
- Previous page: [Uncertainty Sets and Robust Counterparts](introduction.qmd).
- The polyhedral norm behind the budget set, and robust LP under general norms: see @bertsimas2004norms.
  For a survey of the field, see @bertsimas2011.
